pedagogy.summary: At 6-8, pictograms, tally charts and block diagrams are the first FORMAL data representations — each is a translation of counts into a picture and back. The child must both READ one (what does this tell us? how many?) and CONSTRUCT one from their own data. The load-bearing ideas are the tally's grouping in fives, the pictogram's key (one symbol standing for one — or, as this extends, for several) and the block diagram's equal, aligned blocks on a common baseline so height means count. Teaching should build charts from data the children collected, make the key/one-to-one correspondence explicit, and move back and forth between the picture and the numbers (Curcio's 'reading the data').
bestPractices: Construct each chart from the class's own tallied data so the picture is grounded in counts they made
Make the key explicit and read it first ('one apple picture = one child'), previewing many-to-one keys (2, 5, 10) as a deliberate step
Draw tallies in gated fives and count in fives, and keep pictogram symbols and blocks equal-sized and aligned to a baseline so height/length is trustworthy
Ask both directions: read a value off a given chart, then add a new category to it — so interpreting and constructing reinforce each other
keyRepresentations: Pictogram with an explicit key (symbols aligned in rows)
Block diagram / block graph on a common baseline
Simple table linking category to frequency
commonMisconceptions: Reads each pictogram symbol as 'one' when the key says it stands for several (ignores the key / many-to-one)
Counts tally marks one-by-one and miscounts, or draws the fifth mark as a fifth upright instead of the diagonal gate
Misreads a block diagram or pictogram by length when blocks/symbols are unequal or not aligned to a baseline
Constructs a chart with uneven gaps, unequal symbols, or no key, so it cannot be read back accurately

learn.summary: For ages 6-8, pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams and simple tables are the first formal data representations: each turns counts into a picture (or table) and back again. Learners should both read a given chart (what does this tell us? how many?) and construct one from data they collected. The load-bearing ideas are the tally's grouping in gated fives, the pictogram's key (one symbol standing for one, later for several), and a block diagram's equal, aligned blocks on a common baseline so that height/length means count. Move deliberately between picture and numbers in both directions.

activities.title: Two-way chart builder from the class's own data
feedback: When a read-back answer is correct, highlighting the matching row/blocks confirms which part of the chart was being counted
If the learner just counts symbols after the key changes to 2 per symbol, point out that the same row now means double and ask them to re-read the key before answering
If blocks are uneven or not on a baseline, recount to show that the taller row is not always 'more' unless the units are equal and aligned to a common baseline
activities.rationale: Year 2 pupils are expected to interpret AND construct simple pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams and tables, and non-statutory guidance introduces many-to-one keys with ratios of 2, 5 and 10; building from the children's own tallied data grounds the picture in counts they made. An interactive builder is one way that may make the picture-to-number translation and the key's power concrete, with immediate feedback; paper tallies, printed symbols, a drawn table and a drawn baseline can achieve the same objective.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils interpret and construct simple pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams and tables; non-statutory guidance introduces many-to-one correspondence in pictograms with simple ratios of 2, 5 and 10
learnerActions: Collect or be given a stream of survey results (e.g. favourite pets) and record them as tally marks, forming gated fives (four uprights with a diagonal fifth) and counting in fives
Also record the counts in a simple table linking each category to its frequency
Stamp or draw pictogram symbols into aligned rows next to an explicit key, reading the key first: 'one picture = one child'
Answer read-back questions such as 'how many children chose dogs?' and check against the highlighted row
Flip the key to 'one picture = 2' and re-state what the same row now means, then construct a new row from a given count under that key
Rebuild the data as a block diagram with equal-sized blocks aligned to a common baseline
activities.intendedInsight: A chart or table is a reversible translation between counts and a picture; the key governs what each symbol is worth, and height/length can only be trusted when units are equal and aligned to a baseline.

activities.title: Many-to-one key: read through it and reverse it
feedback: If the learner answers with the raw number of symbols, they have ignored the key; read the key aloud first and overlay a one-to-one version to show each symbol 'carries' 2
If the learner draws 6 symbols for 6 fish under a key of 2, show that this would actually represent 12, then rebuild the row from the key (3 symbols)
A correct response states the frequency, explains that the key was used, and handles a half-symbol as half the key value (with a key of 2, half a symbol = 1)
activities.rationale: Some sources use 'picture graph' for charts with one object per individual and 'pictograph' for charts where a symbol represents several items, but these terms are not used consistently, and in UK usage both are called pictograms. The key distinction is one-to-one versus many-to-one keys. This underlies many-to-one key reading, and reversing it (count to symbols) is what separates genuine understanding from symbol-counting.
sourceClaims: A picture graph uses one object to represent one individual, whereas a pictograph uses a symbol to represent SEVERAL items in a category — the distinction underlying many-to-one key reading; displays (tables, picture graphs, bar graphs) represent the distribution of a categorical variable
learnerActions: Read a pictogram whose key says one picture stands for 2 pets, and state how many children have a dog, explaining how the key was used
Interpret a half-symbol under the key: say how many it represents and justify your answer
Reverse the direction: given a tally showing 6 fish, draw the pictogram row using the same key, deciding how many whole symbols are needed
Given that existing fish row, show how it would change if 3 more fish joined, keeping to the same key
Compare a pictogram where one symbol means one individual with a pictogram where one symbol stands for several, and say which key is in use
activities.intendedInsight: The key must be applied, not assumed: a many-to-one pictogram is read as symbols times the key value, and constructing a row reverses that (6 fish become 3 symbols under a key of 2); updating a count means changing the number of symbols by the added count divided by the key value (3 more fish under a key of 2 means 1½ more symbols, so 9 fish = 4½ symbols).

activities.title: Check for value-by-length and tally errors
feedback: If the learner calls the furthest-reaching row 'most' when its symbols are bigger or fewer, return to equal blocks on a common baseline and recount
If tallies are counted in ones and slip, model gated fives and counting in fives — treat this as a recording/counting lapse to steady, not a conceptual reteach
If a constructed chart has uneven gaps, unequal symbols or no key, it cannot be read back; fix one element at a time and re-read
activities.rationale: Common errors are reading by raw length when units are unequal and miscounting tallies; equal aligned units on a baseline and gated fives are the fixes. Distinguishing a recording lapse from a conceptual misread guides whether to steady technique or reteach equal-unit reasoning.
learnerActions: Look at a block diagram or pictogram where blocks/symbols are unequal or off the baseline and decide whether the longest row really is 'most', stating what you would check
Count a set of tally marks that includes ungated or slow one-by-one groups and recount using gated fives
Add a new category to an existing chart and check the chart can still be read back accurately
activities.intendedInsight: Height or length means count only when units are equal and aligned to a common baseline; tallies are counted reliably in gated fives, not one by one.

constraints: Construct each chart from data the children actually tallied so the picture is grounded in counts they made.
Make the key explicit and read it first; preview many-to-one keys (2, 5, 10) as a deliberate step rather than assuming one-to-one.
Keep tally marks in gated fives, and keep pictogram symbols and blocks equal-sized and aligned to a baseline so height/length is trustworthy.
Always ask both directions: read a value off a given chart AND add to or construct a chart (or table), so interpreting and constructing reinforce each other.

A static annotated pictogram (labelling key, symbol, category) is a useful vocabulary reference, but it does not let the learner construct a chart or apply a changing many-to-one key; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
Recognition-only items (e.g. 'how many?' multiple choice) can assess interpretation but do not by themselves elicit the construction/reversal direction; pair them with a draw/build step.
When using a half-symbol, choose a key value such that half is meaningful (e.g. a key of 2 gives a half-symbol = 1).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed that dialogue 'supplies nothing to read or build' and that '3D adds nothing' because these representations are 'inherently flat'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped. Flat displays are the natural medium here, but this does not prove other media add nothing — spoken discussion can still support reading the key and reasoning about equal units, even if it does not itself produce a chart to read or build.

The non-preferred quiz approach (read-off plus a construct-a-row step) and the static annotated pictogram have been preserved as, respectively, an assessment pairing and a vocabulary scaffold rather than discarded.
Half-symbol interpretation is pedagogically reasonable but requires a key value where 'half' maps to a whole item; flagged so authors set the key appropriately.
Whether an interactive builder is more effective than paper tallies/printed symbols for this objective was not tested; both are presented as equivalent means to the objective.

probeDeeper: Ask 'what does one picture stand for here — and how do you know?' to check the key is read, not assumed
Counterexample tuned to this topic: show a half-symbol and ask 'how many is that?' to test whether the key is applied flexibly
Ask 'if 3 more fish joined, how would your row change?' to check the translate direction is secure
Ask 'this block is taller — does that always mean more? what would you check?' to surface equal-unit/baseline reasoning
assess.correctAnswer: Interpreting: uses the key (counts the dog symbols and multiplies by 2, halving for any half-symbol) to state the correct frequency and explains the key was used. Translating: draws 3 whole symbols for 6 fish (because each = 2), aligned in the row — showing the key works both directions.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the key and reads each symbol as one, so a many-to-one pictogram is read at half its value (and constructed with one symbol per item)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the key aloud first every time; overlay the pictogram on a one-to-one version to show each symbol 'carries' 2; rebuild the fish row from the key
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the number of dog symbols as the answer, and draws 6 symbols for 6 fish rather than 3

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts tally marks one-by-one and miscounts, or draws the fifth mark as a fifth upright rather than the diagonal gate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model gated fives and counting in fives; treat as a recording/counting lapse to steady, not a conceptual reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts tallies slowly in ones and slips, or produces ungated groups of five

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads or constructs a block diagram/pictogram by length when blocks or symbols are unequal or off the baseline
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to equal blocks on a common baseline; recount to show height means count only when units are equal — link back to one-to-one sorting/counting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child calls the row that reaches furthest 'most' though its symbols are bigger/fewer, or draws blocks of differing size

responseLevels.gap: Reads symbols/blocks as ones ignoring the key, miscounts tallies, and constructs charts that can't be read back
responseLevels.full: Reads a many-to-one pictogram via the key AND constructs one correctly (e.g. 3 symbols for 6), draws gated tallies and equal aligned blocks, moving fluently between picture and number
responseLevels.partial: Reads and builds one-to-one charts correctly and counts gated tallies, but misapplies a many-to-one key or needs prompting to reverse it when constructing

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First: here is a pictogram of our class's pets with a key saying one picture stands for 2 pets — how many children have a dog, and how did you work it out? Then: here is the tally for fish, showing 6 — draw the pictogram row for fish using the same key.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with representational fluency reads THROUGH the key (symbols × value) and can reverse it to construct a row; a child without it counts symbols as ones when reading, and when drawing puts 6 symbols for 6 fish — the reversal to '3 symbols = 6' is what separates genuine understanding from symbol-counting.
